title: Physics for Beginners
summary: Learn the core ideas of physics with worked calculations: describing motion, forces and Newton's laws, energy, work and power, waves, sound and light, electricity basics, and matter, density and heat.
audience: Secondary students, adult learners, apprentices and anyone curious about how the world works

body.p: Physics explains how the universe behaves, from falling mangoes to orbiting satellites. It begins with describing motion precisely.

list: Speed = distance / time. A bus travelling 120 km in 1.5 hours has an average speed of 80 km/h, about 22.2 m/s (divide km/h by 3.6).
Velocity is speed in a given direction; it is a vector.
Acceleration = change in velocity / time. A car going from 0 to 20 m/s in 5 s accelerates at 4 m/s².
Deceleration is negative acceleration, such as braking.

body.p: On a distance-time graph, the slope is speed; a flat line means the object is stationary. On a velocity-time graph, the slope is acceleration and the area under the line is the distance travelled.
SI units keep calculations consistent: metres (m), seconds (s), kilograms (kg). Convert before calculating.

body.tip: Write the formula, substitute values with units, then calculate; it prevents most mistakes.

body.p: A force is a push or pull, measured in newtons (N). Forces change an object's motion or shape.

list: First law: an object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless a resultant force acts. This is why passengers lurch forward when a taxi brakes suddenly; seatbelts provide the force to stop them.
Second law: F = ma. To accelerate a 1200 kg car at 4 m/s² needs a resultant force of 1200 x 4 = 4800 N.
Third law: for every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force on the other object; a rocket pushes gas backwards and the gas pushes the rocket forwards.

body.p: Weight is the gravitational force on a mass: W = mg, with g about 9.8 N/kg on Earth. A 60 kg person weighs about 588 N; mass stays the same on the Moon, but weight is about one-sixth. Friction opposes motion between surfaces; it lets tyres grip the road but also wastes energy in machines.

body.tip: Draw a force diagram with arrows for every force before solving problems; it shows the resultant force clearly.

body.p: Energy is the ability to do work, measured in joules (J). It cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or changed from one form to another (conservation of energy).

list: Kinetic energy = ½mv². A 1000 kg car at 20 m/s has ½ x 1000 x 20² = 200 000 J.
Gravitational potential energy = mgh. Lifting a 50 kg bag of maize 10 m stores about 50 x 9.8 x 10 = 4900 J.
Work done = force x distance moved in the direction of the force.
Power = energy / time, in watts (W). Lifting that bag in 7 s needs 4900 / 7 = 700 W.

body.p: Efficiency = useful energy out / total energy in x 100%. No real machine is 100% efficient; some energy is always wasted, usually as heat. LED bulbs convert far more electrical energy into light than old incandescent bulbs, which waste most as heat.

body.tip: Track energy through a system as a flow diagram: where it starts, where it goes and where it is wasted.

body.p: Waves transfer energy without transferring matter. In transverse waves (such as light and water waves) the vibrations are at right angles to the direction of travel; in longitudinal waves (such as sound) they are along it.

Wave speed = frequency x wavelength (v = fλ). Sound travels at about 340 m/s in air; a 680 Hz note has a wavelength of 340 / 680 = 0.5 m. Light travels at about 3 x 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum, so radio waves of 100 MHz have a wavelength of about 3 m.

list: Sound needs a medium and cannot travel through a vacuum; it travels faster in solids than in air.
Pitch depends on frequency; loudness on amplitude.
Light reflects from mirrors (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection) and refracts (bends) when it enters glass or water, which is how lenses and eyes focus.
The electromagnetic spectrum includes radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays.

body.tip: Remember the rainbow order of visible light from long to short wavelength: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet.

body.p: Electric current is the flow of charge, measured in amperes (A). Voltage (potential difference), in volts (V), pushes current around a circuit. Resistance, in ohms (Ω), opposes current.

list: Ohm's law: V = IR. A 12 V battery across a 4 Ω resistor drives 12 / 4 = 3 A.
Power: P = VI. That circuit uses 12 x 3 = 36 W.
In series circuits the same current flows through every component and voltages add.
In parallel circuits each branch gets the full voltage and currents add; homes are wired in parallel so appliances work independently.
Conductors (copper, aluminium) let current flow easily; insulators (plastic, rubber) do not.

body.p: Fuses and circuit breakers cut the supply when current is too high; earthing gives fault current a safe path. Never touch mains wiring, keep electricity away from water, and do not overload sockets.

body.tip: Learn V = IR in a triangle (V on top, I and R below); cover the quantity you want to find.

body.p: Matter is made of particles. In solids they vibrate in fixed positions, in liquids they move past each other, and in gases they move freely and fast. Heating gives particles more energy, which can change the state.
Density = mass / volume. A 500 g stone with a volume of 250 cm³ has a density of 2 g/cm³. Objects denser than water (1 g/cm³) sink; less dense objects float.

list: Temperature measures how hot something is; heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference.
Energy needed to warm a substance: Q = mcΔT. Heating 2 kg of water (c = 4200 J/kg°C) by 30 °C needs 2 x 4200 x 30 = 252 000 J.
Heat moves by conduction (through solids), convection (currents in fluids) and radiation (infrared waves, even through a vacuum).
Insulation, such as ceiling boards, reduces unwanted heat transfer.

body.tip: Water's high specific heat capacity is why coastal areas have milder temperatures than inland areas.
